problems.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
problems.description:
You are given an integer array `nums` consisting of `n` elements, and an integer `k`.

Find a contiguous subarray whose **length is exactly `k`** that has the **maximum average value** and return this value. Any answer with a calculation error less than `10^-5` will be accepted.

examples.explanation: The maximum average is (12 - 5 - 6 + 50) / 4 = 51 / 4 = 12.75.
The single element is itself the only subarray of length 1.

edge_cases: Mixed positive and negative summing to zero
problems.approach_brute: For each starting index i in [0, n-k], compute the sum of nums[i..i+k-1] and track the maximum. Time O(N·K), space O(1). Times out when N·K exceeds ~10^7.
problems.approach_optimal: Compute the sum of the first window of size k. Slide the window one step at a time: subtract the leaving element and add the entering element. Track the running maximum sum, then divide by k at the end. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.description:
Given two strings `s` and `p`, return an array of all the **start indices** of `p`'s anagrams in `s`. You may return the answer in any order.

An **Anagram** is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once.

examples.explanation: The substring with start index 0 is "cba", which is an anagram of "abc". The substring with start index 6 is "bac", which is an anagram of "abc".
Starting at indices 0, 1, and 2 we have "ab", "ba", "ab" — all anagrams of "ab".

constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters
problems.approach_brute: For each window of length p.length in s, sort its characters and compare to sorted p. O(N · K log K) where K = p.length. Times out for N = 30000.
problems.approach_optimal: Maintain a frequency array of size 26 for p, and a frequency array for the current window. Initialize on the first window of size p.length, then slide one character at a time: increment the entering char, decrement the leaving char. After each slide, compare the two frequency arrays in O(26). Time O(N), space O(σ).

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.description:
Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a permutation of `s1`, or `false` otherwise.

In other words, return `true` if one of `s1`'s permutations is the substring of `s2`.

examples.explanation: s2 contains one permutation of s1 ("ba").
No permutation of "ab" is a substring of "eidboaoo".

constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters
edge_cases: s1 and s2 are anagrams of each other
problems.approach_brute: Generate all permutations of s1 and check each against s2. O(K! · N) — exponential, infeasible for K > 8.
problems.approach_optimal: Identical structure to 'Find All Anagrams': frequency-count s1, slide a window of length s1.length over s2, compare frequency vectors after each slide. Time O(N), space O(σ).

problems.title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
problems.description:
Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, return the **maximum number of vowel letters** in any substring of `s` with length `k`.

Vowel letters in English are `'a'`, `'e'`, `'i'`, `'o'`, and `'u'`.

examples.explanation: The substring "iii" contains 3 vowel letters.
Any substring of length 2 contains 2 vowels.
"lee", "eet", and "ode" each contain 2 vowels.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
problems.approach_brute: For each window of size k, count vowels by scanning. O(N · K). Times out for N = K = 10^5.
problems.approach_optimal: Slide a window of size k. Maintain a count of vowels in the window. When entering a vowel, increment; when leaving a vowel, decrement. Track the running max. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: Number of Sub-arrays of Size K With Average ≥ Threshold
problems.description: Given an array of integers `arr` and two integers `k` and `threshold`, return the number of subarrays of size `k` and average **greater than or equal to** `threshold`.

examples.explanation: Subarrays [2,5,5], [5,5,5], [5,5,8] have averages 4, 5, 6 respectively. All are >= 4.
All subarrays of size 3 except [7,5,2] and [5,2,3] have averages >= 5.

problems.approach_brute: For each window of size k, compute the sum and compare avg = sum/k against threshold. The naive recomputation is O(N·K).
problems.approach_optimal: Avoid floating-point: compare sum >= k * threshold. Slide a window of size k maintaining its sum incrementally. Increment count whenever sum >= k*threshold. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: Defuse the Bomb
problems.description:
You have a bomb to defuse, and your time is running out! Your informer will provide you with a circular array `code` of length `n` and a key `k`.

To decrypt the code, you must replace every number. All the numbers are replaced **simultaneously**.

- If `k > 0`, replace the i-th number with the **sum of the next k numbers**.
- If `k < 0`, replace the i-th number with the **sum of the previous |k| numbers**.
- If `k == 0`, replace the i-th number with `0`.

As `code` is circular, the next element of `code[n-1]` is `code[0]`, and the previous element of `code[0]` is `code[n-1]`.

Given the **circular** array `code` and an integer key `k`, return the decrypted code.

examples.explanation: Each number is replaced by the sum of the next 3 numbers. The circular nature wraps around.
When k = 0, every number is replaced with 0.
Each number is replaced by the sum of the previous 2 numbers.

problems.approach_brute: For each i, loop |k| steps in the appropriate direction, summing modulo n. O(N · |k|).
problems.approach_optimal: Slide a fixed-size window of width |k| around the circular array. For k > 0, the window for index i covers code[i+1..i+k]. Slide one step at a time updating the sum. For k < 0, mirror the logic. Time O(N), space O(N) for output.

problems.title: Diet Plan Performance
problems.description:
A dieter consumes `calories[i]` calories on the i-th day.

Given an integer `k`, for **every consecutive sequence of `k` days** (`calories[i], calories[i+1], ..., calories[i+k-1]` for all `0 <= i <= n-k`), they look at `T`, the total calories consumed during that sequence of `k` days:

- If `T < lower`, they performed poorly and lose `1` point.
- If `T > upper`, they performed well and gain `1` point.
- Otherwise, they neither gain nor lose any point.

Return the **total number of points** the dieter has after dieting for `calories.length` days.

The total points can be negative.

examples.explanation: Days 1, 2 are below lower (-1 each); day 3 is in range; days 4, 5 are above upper (+1 each). Total = -2 + 0 + 2 = 0.
Sum = 5 > 1, gain +1.

problems.approach_brute: For each window, sum k values from scratch. O(N · K).
problems.approach_optimal: Sliding window of size k with running sum. After each slide, classify the window into −1 / 0 / +1. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: Grumpy Bookstore Owner
problems.description:
There is a bookstore owner that has a store open for `n` minutes. You are given an integer array `customers` of length `n` where `customers[i]` is the number of customers entering the store at minute `i`, and a binary array `grumpy` where `grumpy[i]` is `1` if the bookstore owner is grumpy during minute `i`, and `0` otherwise.

When the bookstore owner is grumpy, the customers of that minute are not satisfied; otherwise, they are satisfied.

The bookstore owner knows a secret technique to keep themselves not grumpy for `minutes` consecutive minutes, but can only use it once.

Return the **maximum number of customers** that can be satisfied throughout the day.

examples.explanation: Use the technique on the last 3 minutes. Naturally satisfied (grumpy=0) = 1+1+1+7=10; gained from technique on minutes 5,6,7 = 1+0+5=6; total = 16.

problems.approach_brute: For each window of size `minutes`, compute total satisfied customers if technique is applied there. O(N · minutes).
problems.approach_optimal: Compute the base satisfied total (sum of customers[i] where grumpy[i] == 0). Then slide a window of size `minutes` over customers[i]·grumpy[i] tracking the max gain. Answer = base + max_gain. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: K Radius Subarray Averages
problems.description:
You are given a 0-indexed array `nums` of `n` integers, and an integer `k`.

The **k-radius average** for a subarray of `nums` centered at some index `i` with the radius `k` is the average of all elements in `nums` between the indices `i - k` and `i + k` (**inclusive**). If there are fewer than `2 * k + 1` elements between these indices, the k-radius average is `-1`.

Build and return an array `avgs` of length `n` where `avgs[i]` is the k-radius average for the subarray centered at index `i`.

The **average** of `x` elements is the sum of the `x` elements divided by `x`, using **integer division**. The integer division truncates toward zero.

examples.explanation: Only indices 3, 4, 5 have a full window of size 7. avgs[3] = floor(37/7) = 5, avgs[4] = floor(32/7) = 4, avgs[5] = floor(34/7) = 4.
Window size = 1, average is the element itself.

problems.approach_brute: For each i, sum nums[i-k..i+k] from scratch. O(N · K). Times out when N·K exceeds 10^7.
problems.approach_optimal: Window size is `2k+1`. Slide it once across nums. Indices in [k, n-k-1] get a real average; others get -1. Use a 64-bit running sum to avoid overflow on max-value inputs. Time O(N), space O(N) for output.

problems.title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
problems.description:
There are several cards arranged in a row, and each card has an associated number of points. The points are given in the integer array `cardPoints`.

In one step, you can take **one card from the beginning or from the end of the row**. You have to take exactly `k` cards.

Your score is the sum of the points of the cards you have taken.

Given the integer array `cardPoints` and the integer `k`, return the **maximum score** you can obtain.

examples.explanation: Take the last three cards (6,1) and one more from the front gives best: 1+6+5=12 by taking front 1, then 6 and 5 from the back? Actually take from back: 1, 6, 5 → sum = 12.
Regardless of which two cards you choose, the score is 4.

edge_cases: Highly skewed values at one end
problems.approach_brute: Try every split: take i from the front and k-i from the back, compute total, track max. O(K) overall but cleanly correct. Note: this *is* the canonical approach since K can be up to N.
problems.approach_optimal: Equivalent reformulation: minimize the sum of the (n-k) contiguous cards left in the middle. Slide a window of size n-k and find its minimum sum. Answer = total_sum - min_window_sum. Both approaches are O(N).

problems.title: Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters
problems.description:
A string is **good** if there are no repeated characters.

Given a string `s`, return the number of **good substrings of length three** in `s`.

Note that if there are multiple occurrences of the same substring, every occurrence should be counted.

A **substring** is a contiguous sequence of characters in a string.

examples.explanation: Substrings of length 3: "xyz", "yzz", "zza", "zaz". Only "xyz" has all distinct characters.
Good substrings: "abc", "bca", "cab", "abc" — 4 in total.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
problems.approach_brute: For each window of size 3, check that the 3 characters are pairwise distinct. O(N) trivially.
problems.approach_optimal: Same as brute since the window is a fixed tiny size — three pairwise comparisons per window. Time O(N), space O(1).

problems.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
problems.description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`, where `nums[i]` represents the score of the i-th student. You are also given an integer `k`.

Pick the scores of any `k` students from the array so that the **difference between the highest and the lowest** of the `k` scores is **minimized**.

Return the **minimum possible difference**.

examples.explanation: Pick the only score; difference is 0.
Sorted: [1,4,7,9]. Closest pair is (7,9) with difference 2.

problems.approach_brute: Try all C(n, k) subsets; track min(max - min). Exponential, infeasible.
problems.approach_optimal: Sort the array. The optimal k-subset is a *contiguous* segment of the sorted array (any non-contiguous choice has a strictly worse spread). Slide a window of size k and minimize sorted[i+k-1] − sorted[i]. Time O(N log N), space O(1).
